In mathematics, the '''Hermite''' or '''Pólya class''' is a [[set (mathematics)|set]] of [[entire function]]s satisfying the requirement that if ''E(z)'' is in the class, then:<ref>{{cite book|title=Hilbert spaces of entire functions|url=https://archive.org/details/hilbertspacesofe0000debr|url-access=registration|year=1968|publisher=Prentice-Hall|location=London|isbn=978-0133889000|author=Louis de Branges|authorlink=Louis de Branges de Bourcia}}</ref><ref name="Kalt">[http://asc.tuwien.ac.at/funkana/woracek/papers/polya.pdf "Polya class theory for Hermite-Biehler functions of finite order"] by [[Michael Kaltenbäck]] and [[Harald Woracek]], ''[[J. London Math. Soc.]]'' (2) 68.2 (2003), pp. 338–354. {{doi|10.1112/S0024610703004502}}.</ref>

#''E(z)'' has no zero ([[root of a function|root]]) in the [[upper half-plane]].
#<math>|E(x+iy)|\ge|E(x-iy)|</math> for ''x'' and ''y'' real and ''y'' positive.
#<math>|E(x+iy)|</math> is a [[non-decreasing function]] of ''y'' for positive ''y''.

The first condition (no root in the upper half plane) can be derived from the third plus a condition that the function not be identically zero. The second condition is not implied by the third, as demonstrated by the function <math>\exp(-iz+e^{iz}).</math> In at least one publication of [[Louis de Branges]], the second condition is replaced by a strict inequality, which modifies some of the properties given below.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Louis de Branges|title=The Convergence of Euler Products|journal=[[Journal of Functional Analysis]]|volume=107|pages=122–210|date=Jul 1992|doi=10.1016/0022-1236(92)90103-P|author1-link=Louis de Branges|doi-access=}}</ref>

Every entire function of Hermite class can be expressed as the limit of a series of polynomials having no zeros in the upper half-plane.<ref>{{cite web|title=A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis|url=http://www.math.purdue.edu/~branges/riemannzeta.pdf|author=Louis de Branges|authorlink=Louis de Branges de Bourcia|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20061109052212/http://www.math.purdue.edu/~branges/riemannzeta.pdf|archivedate=November 9, 2006|page=6}}</ref>

The product of two functions of Hermite class is also of Hermite class, so the class constitutes a [[monoid]] under the operation of multiplication of functions.

The class arises from investigations by [[Georg Pólya]] in 1913<ref>G. Polya: "Über Annäherung durch Polynome mit lauter reellen Wurzeln", Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 36 (1913), 279-295.</ref> but some prefer to call it the Hermite class after [[Charles Hermite]].<ref>De Branges used the term Pólya class until at least 2006 but later preferred the term Hermite class. See his 2017 draft,[https://web.archive.org/web/20170516180552/http://www.math.purdue.edu/~branges/proof-riemann-2017-04.pdf The Riemann Hypothesis].</ref>
A [[de Branges space]] can be defined on the basis of some "[[Weight function]]" of Hermite class, but with the additional stipulation that the inequality be strict – that is, <math>|E(x+iy)|>|E(x-iy)|</math> for positive ''y''. (However, a de Branges space can be defined using a function that is not in the class, such as {{math|exp(''z''<sup>2</sup>−''iz'')}}.)

The Hermite class is a subset of the ''[[Hermite–Biehler class]]'', which does not include the third of the above three requirements.<ref name=Kalt/>

A function with no roots in the upper half plane is of Hermite class [[if and only if]] two conditions are met: that the nonzero roots ''z<sub>n</sub>'' satisfy

:<math>\sum_n\frac{1-\operatorname{Im} z_n}{|z_n|^2}<\infty</math>

(with roots counted according to their [[multiplicity (mathematics)#Multiplicity of a root of a polynomial|multiplicity]]), and that the function can be expressed in the form of a [[Hadamard product (entire functions)|Hadamard product]]

:<math>z^m e^{a+bz+cz^2}\prod_n \left(1-z/z_n\right)\exp(z\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{z_n})</math>

with ''c'' real and non-positive and Im ''b'' non-positive. (The non-negative integer ''m'' will be positive if ''E''(0)=0. Even if the number of roots is infinite, the [[infinite product]] is well defined and converges.<ref>Section 7 of the book by de Branges.</ref>) From this we can see that if a function {{math|''f''(''z'')}} of Hermite class has a root at {{mvar|w}}, then <math>f(z)/(z-w)</math> will also be of Hermite class.

Assume {{math|''f''(''z'')}} is a non-constant polynomial of Hermite class. If its derivative is zero at some point {{mvar|w}} in the upper half-plane, then
:<math>|f(z)|\sim|f(w)+a(z-w)^n|</math>
near {{mvar|w}} for some complex number {{mvar|a}} and some integer {{mvar|n}} greater than 1. But this would imply that <math>|f(x+iy)|</math> decreases with {{mvar|y}} somewhere in any neighborhood of {{mvar|w}}, which cannot be the case. So the derivative is a polynomial with no root in the upper half-plane, that is, of Hermite class. Since a non-constant function of Hermite class is the [[limit of a sequence]] of such polynomials, its derivative will be of Hermite class as well.<ref>This is Problem 17 in de Branges's book. Solutions to some of the Problems in the book can be found in [https://web.archive.org/web/20150514020454/http://www.its.caltech.edu/~dlinghu/research/index_files/dB-problems.pdf Solution to "Hilbert Spaces of Entire Functions"] by Kevin Linghu.</ref>

[[Louis de Branges]] showed a connexion between functions of Hermite class and [[analytic function]]s whose imaginary part is non-negative in the [[upper half-plane]] (UHP), often called [[Nevanlinna function]]s. If a function ''E''(''z'') is of Hermite-Biehler class and ''E''(0) = 1, we can take the [[logarithm]] of ''E'' in such a way that it is analytic in the UHP and such that log(''E''(0)) = 0. Then ''E''(''z'') is of Hermite class if and only if

:<math>\text{Im}\frac{-\log(E(z))}z\ge 0</math>

(in the UHP).<ref>Section 14 of the book by de Branges, or {{cite journal|title=Some applications of spaces of entire functions|journal=[[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]]|year=1963|volume=15|pages=563–83|doi=10.4153/CJM-1963-058-1|author=Louis de Branges|s2cid=247198147 }}</ref>

==Laguerre–Pólya class==
A smaller class of entire functions is the [[Laguerre–Pólya class]], which consists of those functions which are locally the limit of a series of polynomials whose roots are all real. Any function of Laguerre–Pólya class is also of Hermite class. Some examples are <math>\sin(z), \cos(z), \exp(z), \text{ and }\exp(-z^2).</math>

==Examples==
From the Hadamard form it is easy to create examples of functions of Hermite class. Some examples are:
*A non-zero constant.
*<math>z</math>
*Polynomials having no roots in the upper half plane, such as <math>z+i</math>
*<math>\exp(-piz)</math> if and only if Re(''p'') is non-negative
*<math>\exp(-pz^2)</math> if and only if ''p'' is a non-negative real number
*any function of Laguerre-Pólya class: <math>\sin(z), \cos(z), \exp(z), \exp(-z), \exp(-z^2).</math>
*A product of functions of Hermite class
